video_title: Chris Webber compares Wemby to this ALL TIME GREAT! | The Rich Eisen Show

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Vlade Divac's flopping technique and its effectiveness
quotes.excerpt: He may have invented the flop. I mean, he did have an art to it.

text_blocks.speaker: Susie Schuster
text_blocks.text: I did make a joke yesterday, we're doing biggest flops. I did my top five all-time flops and I did put Vlade in, I think as number three. Thoughts on Vlade as a flopper?

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: Yeah, he's one of the best passers I've played with and, you know, I definitely get what you're saying from that point of view. He may have invented the flop. I mean, he did have an art to it.

text_blocks.speaker: Susie Schuster
text_blocks.text: He may have invented the flop. I mean, he did have an art to it.

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: He did, and one thing, you know, with Shaq, if you're flopping a little bit, Shaq is so strong, you know, it's going to make you look like you're really flopping. But, you know, I think Vlade, you know, would admit that, but he always played the game with integrity and, you know, and as hard as he could. So, yeah, he did flop a little bit though.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber recalls the NBA's era of dominant power forwards
quotes.excerpt: I grew up in the era of the power forwards, so if you could imagine.
quotes.quote: For me, you know, it was the power forwards. I grew up in the era of the power forwards, so if you could imagine, it would be for me like just the schedule. So on a Monday, Tuesday, I could have KG and Tim back-to-back, with Karl Malone on Thursday, with Shaq on Saturday. So it was just, you know, I loved the way that, when I played, it was a power forwards, you know, kind of league. And so for me, from Dirk, there's so many guys, I don't want to miss anyone, but Glenn Robinson, Vin Baker at the time. So, of course it would probably be Tim and KG, but really you had to be prepared every night and couldn't make anyone your favorite because you'd get your, you'd get busted up in you.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber recounts dunking on his hero Charles Barkley as a rookie
quotes.excerpt: I made sure I looked up at my pops and I was like, 'What do you think about your hero now?'

text_blocks.speaker: Susie Schuster
text_blocks.text: And then I'm sure you saw on the Inside guys the other night if you dunking on Charles. Do you remember that at all?

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: Yeah, I definitely remember it because I was such a big fan of Chuck. And I met him in high school and I was a rookie, so I flew my whole family out to the game and, you know, my father, my brothers were teasing me that your hero's going to get you tonight. And so as soon as I dunked on him, I made sure I looked up at my pops and I was like, 'What do you think about your hero now?'

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: But, but, you know, and I tell Charles that all the time and then he comes back with, 'Don Nelson, we didn't double him in the playoffs.' And so, that means Charles gave us something like 54 in the playoffs because he was pissed about the commercial that we made about dunking.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber explains how dunks provide momentum beyond two points
quotes.excerpt: It gives a momentum to a team and it adds so much that so many intangibles.
quotes.quote: I think a lot of people always said that a dunk, you know, was only worth two points, but I really never believed that because it gives a momentum, it gives a momentum to a team and it adds so much that so many intangibles that, you know, that you really can't even articulate because it's in the spur of the moment. It's who you're playing against. I guarantee you, you know, if someone dunked on Wembanyama, that team is going to play more energetically from that moment on. And so for me, you know, watching these guys go at it and, you know, watching them play is nothing like attacking the rim and and catching a body, whether it's D-Wade, LeBron, you know, Jordan used to do it all the time, but it, but it's still to me a big part of the game.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber emphasizes playoff pain is crucial for young teams to win championships
quotes.excerpt: Usually it has to be some pain on the other side of that championship.
quotes.quote: I was impressed by Oklahoma. You know, we've always seen a team have to go through another team to win a championship. Even if you go way back, and it's funny, Mike Wilbon talks about this all the time, but if you go back to, let's just say, the Pistons going through the Celtics, going through the Lakers, and the teams that the Lakers had to go through. And for me, a young team like this, and I picked the Spurs to win it all this year in the beginning of the season. And the reason why I am wrong and what I was worried about the whole time was that usually it has to be some pain on the other side of that championship. You know, whether it's Shaq in Orlando and then coming to LA doing his thing and then going to Miami, whether it's other players, you see them on the precipice, they lose there, and it, you know, makes for such a big moment. And I think the San Antonio as a team may be in that position where they have to revisit it because the playoffs are just a different monster. You saw how Wemby got pushed around yesterday and I think he was only four for 15. That happens to the best of us.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Wembanyama needs to learn strategic play and involve teammates in the playoffs
quotes.excerpt: He's going to have to learn when to just be in the paint, when to just be a decoy.
quotes.quote: He's going to have to learn when to just be in the paint, when to just be a decoy. He's going to have to learn, you know, when to get other guys involved. And you can't learn unless you have experience, right? And they don't have that experience in the playoffs. And so for me, I'm more impressed with OKC because they did what they were supposed to do. They've been in this position, they're champions, they know how important this game shift is. And so I was impressed that they came through and SGA, I mean, he's, you know, he's, he's still one of the best and him getting guys involved, but him knocking down those open shots was just something crazy.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber advocates for defenders to stay on their feet against flopping
quotes.excerpt: Everybody needs to stay on their feet. Like we have to start criticizing the guard that's defending him.

text_blocks.speaker: Susie Schuster
text_blocks.text: So why would he possibly stay on his feet if he can flop and get the call?

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: You know what, it's funny. I, since, you know, I was on here with Rich, we talked about flopping and I was talking about Embiid, right? Because he was so much bigger. And I didn't even think SGA and everybody's calling me, killing me saying, 'But look at this guy, look at this guy.' I would, I would say this. It's on the refs and he should try to play the way that he can, but everybody needs to stay on their feet. Everybody needs to stay on their feet. Like we have to start criticizing the guard that's defending him. Stay down. Like, don't even make it a chance for the ref. Remember a couple of years ago, I think it, I, I forgot, maybe it was Quin Snyder or another coach, they had guys play with their hands behind their back checking Harden. Remember that? I mean, you have to adjust. And so, I, I get that he, I get, I get it, whatever everyone says, but at the same time, you know, I played against Allen Iverson, he averaged 10 free throws a game. Kobe, 10 free throws a game. So all these guys always had high free throw attempts, but if you're a guard playing against them, stay on your feet and make him earn it.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Wembanyama must dominate inside like Shaq to pressure opponents
quotes.excerpt: If you're the tallest player on the floor, you should probably dominate.
quotes.quote: And then it gets back to the fundamentals of dominating, right? If you're, if you're the tallest player on the floor, you should probably dominate. And that's what Shaq used to do and it puts pressure, pressure, every play on you to where everybody has to respond to the dominance of this guy inside. And that's the level, I know that Wembanyama is going to reach. Dominance, dominance. And, you know, it's not, it's about being uncomfortable, it's about getting better. And so I would love to see him shoot 15 jump hooks tomorrow. I mean, if he's inside at 7'4" and turns around and shoots a jump hook, I mean, it's probably going to go in. And so, you know, when you get, when you get desperate in those moments, you go to your sweet spots and I expect him to go to the pick and roll, attack the basket, get to his sweet spots. And I expect San Antonio to, to win rather handedly because they know how much it, it means to close out games, it are the hardest and, um, you know, they'll have to go see OKC back at home.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber reflects on the controversial Kings-Lakers Game 6 and losing Game 7
quotes.excerpt: You knew something was off at the end of that game. It was the only game I'd ever played where you felt something's off.

text_blocks.speaker: TJ
text_blocks.text: Chris, I just wanted to remind you one thing, Cowboys do have five Super Bowls. But anyway, that's not, that's not what I want to talk to you about. You brought something up that you wanted to tell Susie's daughter, Taylor. You brought up a playoff game between the Kings and the Lakers. Allegedly, there was some, maybe some shady stuff going on. I don't want to get, you know, sued or anything, but can I take you back to that Game 6, brother? Like, do you remember what was going through your, you and your teammates' minds as that game was going on? Were you guys kind of like, something felt off, something didn't feel right?

text_blocks.speaker: Susie Schuster
text_blocks.text: Was that the Rick Fox, Doug Christie fight?

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: No, that was good. That was another story. That was good. No, that was pre-game. Shaq and I, next time Shaq comes on, ask him about that because I always laugh and I tell him, you know, I beat up one of my teammates' wives because she was hitting him in the head. But he laughs about it. But yeah, we, we, you know, you, you knew something was off at the end of that game. It was the only game I'd ever played where, you know, in the back you, you felt something's off. And, uh, so yeah, that was, that was terrible. And, you know, very honestly, so it's terrible, terrible, terrible, right? And Susie, you said play on. And and to me, um, you guys said play on and to me that's what we have to do. We had Game 7 and we did not execute, we didn't hit from the free throw line, we lost the game. And so that game mattered and it took it and it stole it. However, we had another chance and we didn't play our best in that game. And so I can never, you know, blame not having one just on that game, even though, you know, as I used to joke with Kobe all the time that, you know, he might as well let me hold that ring because that was ours, but we still had another chance to, to win and we, we didn't take advantage of it.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber cherishes playing against the best in the Kings-Lakers series
quotes.excerpt: Playing against the best, playing against Shaq and Kobe and Phil Jackson, knowing their dominance.
quotes.quote: My favorite memory from those series are playing against the best, playing against Shaq and Kobe and Phil Jackson, knowing their dominance and knowing what it would take to beat them. And we felt whoever was going to win that was going to win that series. The West Coast was dominant at that time. So the competition and probably the energy.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber praises Sacramento Kings fans' sincere and loyal support
quotes.excerpt: They were there every night, they were there before our team came in... they were there long after.
quotes.quote: Sacramento, you know, it's like a second home and I love it so much there and it's because of the people. We matured there together, it was us against the world there together. You know, those type of things you don't take lightly and representing the small city against big brother in LA. So for me, I remember playing against the best and being with some of the best fans there in the NBA because it was sincere, they were there every night, they were there before our team came in with me, Jason Williams, Vlade and Peja. They were there long after. And so it's true loyalty and, you know, that's the only thing you hate and you love about sports is that I wanted to win because I wanted one, but I definitely wanted to give the fans of a small town one to let them talk because, you know, I want them to feel like, you know, just like the New York fans are going crazy. And that's why, you know, I love seeing the fan experience. It's nothing like it and we felt it as players.

quotes.speaker: Chris Webber
quotes.summary_phrase: Chris Webber clarifies Jason Williams' daughter's athleticism comes from her mom
quotes.excerpt: She gets her athletic ability from the mom. The mom's a track star.

text_blocks.speaker: Susie Schuster
text_blocks.text: By the way, did you see that J-Will's daughter is like a star softball player now with Florida? We're talking, we're going to break her all down tomorrow on Women's Sports Now, because like, somebody said to me, 'Did you realize that's Jason Williams' daughter?' So I like did a little deep dive. I mean, she is balling, it's crazy.

text_blocks.speaker: Chris Webber
text_blocks.text: I just want to say this because J-Will is my brother and his wife is my sister. So, she gets her athletic ability from the mom. The mom's a track star. Okay? So let's get it, let's get it straight. Jason, Jason's all right. He's one of the best, you know, passers ever, but, you know, his daughter, she's cold. And so I think she gets that from mom.
